title: VB9-10139
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He is appealing a Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision that found he was not entitled to refugee protection on the grounds that he had an internal flight alternative (IFA)-a place where he would be safe and where it would be reasonable for him to relocate to-in Merida, Mexico.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Andres or Appellant) is a citizen of Mexico. He is appealing a Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision that found he was not entitled to refugee protection on the grounds that he had an internal flight alternative (IFA)-a place where he would be safe and where it would be reasonable for him to relocate to-in Merida, Mexico.
On this appeal, XXXX makes various arguments to the effect that the RPD erred in finding that he will be safe in Merida.
I am not persuaded by XXXX arguments that the RPD erred in its decision. XXXX has not established that he does not have an IFA in Merida. He is therefore not entitled to refugee protection.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.

XXXX has not taken issue with the RPD's summary of his allegations, as follows:2 [8] The claimant, who is now XXXX years old alleges fear from a Mexican cartel which he believes to be the Familia Michoacana. It started back in XXXX 2015 when he and his brother XXXX were working at his father's store in Tlalnepantla, near Mexico City and two unknown men came into the store and handed them a cell phone. Later that day they received a phone call telling them to hand over XXXX XXXX XXXX pesos if they didn't want something to happen to them. [9] The claimant and his brother decided to throw away the cell phone; the men returned and the claimant and his brother told them they did not have the money. Their father shut down the store for about 10 days. Nothing further happened with respect to this specific threat. [10] On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, the claimant and his brother, XXXX XXXX were celebrating a birthday of one of their cousins at the house of the claimant's parents in Tlalnepantla. XXXX and his wife were leaving to go see a friend, when just as he got outside he was shot in the back five times by a person the claimant believes to be affiliated with the cartel and who goes by the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX was taken to the hospital where he died shortly after. [11] The claimant believes his brother's death and the extortion attempt at the family store are related in part because they were relatively close in time and in part because of the rumours that he had heard about the cartel being involved and XXXX connection to the cartel. He also indicated that his brother had applied to be a police officer but had been overheard telling people that the Quinientos Cartel, which he believes is affiliated with the Familia Michoacana, was investing money in the campaign of the mayor at the time. The claimant alleges that this was also part of the reason for his brother's killing. [12] The claimant took his wife and children to stay in Veracruz for about one and a half to two months to live with his aunt because he believed he was in danger. While in Veracruz, the claimant's aunt heard that four men in a car were said to be asking about the claimant. [13] She felt could no longer house the claimant because of that so the claimant went back to Mexico State, to Vallejo (which is also a neighbourhood in Mexico City), and lived with his in-laws. He says he locked himself in for about six months. [14] After that period of time, things were quiet and the claimant went back to work in Tlalnepantla. [15] The claimant did not report the killing to the police despite claiming to know who the killer was. When asked why, the claimant said he didn't see the point because the police protect "them." The authorities did show up at his parents' house but as far as an investigation into his brother's killing the claimant said there wasn't one. [16] The claimant was able to go about his daily life without incident for approximately two years until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 when the claimant was visiting his ill father and his parent's house. While there, he heard a loud noise, his mother told him to run and the claimant fled. He bought a ticket to Canada and arrived here on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. [17] The claimant fears returning to Mexico because he believes what happened to his brother will happen to him.

XXXX has submitted and requested that the following documents be accepted as new evidence for this appeal: a. A Yucatan Times article entitled, "The renowned Mayan activist, Pedro Uc, was threatened with death in Yucatan; the alleged hit men also threatened to kill his family" (with a date of January 12, 2020, referenced at the end of the article), submitted with the Appellant's Record on January 21, 2020;3 b. A CBC News article entitled, "Homicide charge laid in stabbing death of Canadian man in Mexico", last updated April 23, 2019 (printed January 12, 2020), submitted with the Appellant's Record on January 21, 2020;4 and, c. A letter from XXXX representative dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020, along with a WhatsApp Message and English transcript of same, all of which was submitted on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020.
For the reasons that follow, I am not admitting this evidence.

The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)5 anticipates that an appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) will ordinarily be based on the record of the RPD proceeding. According to the law,6 I can only accept new evidence on this appeal that: i. arose after the RPD decision (the RPD hearing took place on November 7, 2019, and the RPD issued its decision on November 26, 2019); ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD decision; or, iii. that XXXX could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before its decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.7

As provided under Rules 29 and 37 of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules),8 a person who does not provide a document or written submissions with their Appellant's Record must not use the document unless allowed by the RAD. A person must make an application in accordance with RAD Rule 37, and, must show that the documents meet the criteria for acceptance of new evidence under section 110(4) of the IRPA. In deciding the application, the RAD must consider any relevant factors, including the document's relevance and probative value, any new evidence the document brings to the appeal, and whether the person who is the subject of the appeal, with reasonable effort, could have provided the document or written submissions with their record.

The Yucatan Times article is rejected as new evidence because XXXX has not provided any submissions with respect to how this document meets the requirements set out in section 110(4) of the IRPA. I acknowledge that there is a date of January 12, 2020 at the end of the article, but there is no indication whether this is the date of the article or the date that it was printed. The date of January 12, 2020 is the same date that the CBC News article was printed, so it may well be referencing the date that the Yucatan Times article was printed. If it was the date of the article, then I would expect it to appear at the top of the article, as is the consistent practice of other news articles. All of this is to point out that it is not clear, and I have no submissions to explain whether this document arose after the RPD decision; was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD decision; or, that XXXX could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before its decision.

The CBC News article is rejected as new evidence because I have not been provided any submissions to explain how this article meets the requirements of section 110(4) of the IRPA. The header information on the printout of this article indicates that XXXX printed it out on January 12, 2020. However, the relevant date I must consider is the date of the article referenced at the beginning of the article, as is common with news articles, and that date is April 23, 2019. This article did not arise after the RPD decision, but instead arose well before the RPD decision. As the article is from CBC News, a public website, I can see no reasons why this was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD decision; or, that XXXX could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before its decision.

The representative's letter and WhatsApp message and translation are rejected as new evidence. These documents were filed after the Appellant's Record. XXXX has not complied with the requirements of Rules 29 and 37. The letter of February 1, 2020, from his representative does not constitute an affidavit or statutory declaration, as referenced in Rule 37(4). It is odd that the representative is providing evidence (i.e., describing what happened to XXXX XXXX by way of the letter of February 1, 2020, rather than XXXX himself providing that evidence. With respect to the criteria in Rule 29(4), I do not find this WhatsApp message relevant or probative. The English translation of the message indicates, "Now you are fucked, you and your family we got to know that you have been talking if anything happens to our organization we are going to kill them all watch out when you get back." I do not find this message relevant or probative because there is no indication who sent the message. There is no indication concerning the identity of the "organization" referenced. There is no indication that the sender has the motivation or ability to track XXXX to the proposed IFA. The evidence does not bring anything new to the appeal. The threat is so vague that it does not bring any new evidence to the appeal, in terms of whether XXXX faces any likelihood of harm in the proposed IFA. It is unclear whether XXXX with reasonable effort could have provided the message with his Appellant's Record. There is a date on the message of "XXXX XXXX" but no reference to the year. The representative's letter which accompanies the message does not provide a year of when the referenced events took place (the letter is dated February 1, 2020, but the events described in the letter do not reference a year). Again, the letter is not sworn evidence, and in any event, the timing of the events described in the letter is vague. For example, the letter states that XXXX came to the see the representative demanding help, but does not indicate when XXXX came to see her. The letter also indicates that XXXX family members have been "recently" contacted, but provides no specific date. The letter discusses XXXX interaction with his roommates, but provides no specific dates for these events.
Having not admitted any documents under section 110(4) of IRPA, I am unable to order a new hearing under section 110(6) of IRPA.

XXXX has failed to meet the burden of establishing that he does not have an IFA in Merida. For the following reasons, I am not persuaded by his arguments that the RPD erred in its decision that XXXX has an IFA in Merida.

There is a two-prong test to determine whether there is an IFA.9 In order to find that XXXX has an IFA in Merida, first I must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of him being persecuted (section 96 of the IRPA), or that he would not be personally subjected to a danger described in paragraph 97(1)(a), or to a risk described in paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA, in the proposed IFA. Second, I must determine that in all of the circumstances, including the circumstances particular to XXXX, conditions in the part of the country where a potential IFA has been identified are such that it would not be objectively unreasonable for him to seek refuge there before seeking protection in Canada.

The RPD member correctly gave notice to XXXX at the RPD hearing that Merida was being proposed as an IFA.10 After providing such notice, the burden of proof with respect to the two-prong IFA test then rested with XXXX.11

On this appeal, XXXX submissions as to why he believes the RPD erred in its decision centre around the first prong of the IFA test (i.e., whether, on a balance of probabilities, there is no serious possibility of him being persecuted in Merida (section 96 of the IRPA), or that he would not be personally subjected to a danger described in paragraph 97(1)(a), or to a risk described in paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA).

The RPD member noted that based on the evidence, she was unable to find that the alleged risk XXXX faces in Mexico has a link to any of the Convention grounds of race, religion, nationality, particular social group, or political opinion.12 XXXX argues that, "The evidence presented to the RPD by The Appellant clearly shows that The Cartel In Mexico has link to The Convention grounds of a Particular group persecution (a threat to life or freedom)".13 I do not accept XXXX argument for the following reasons. XXXX must establish that he falls into one of the Convention grounds referred to in section 96 of the IRPA, and that there would be a serious possibility of persecution of him by reason of such Convention ground in the proposed IFA of Merida. He has not shown this, and the evidence does not support it.

The RPD noted that with respect to the safety of the IFA, XXXX does not know who tried to extort him and his brother. The RPD indicated that XXXX said the killer of his brother was a person named XXXX, and he believes the agents of harm might be part of the Michoacana cartel, but was only basing that on rumour.14 The RPD noted that XXXX had not sufficiently established that those who were involved in the extortion attempt and/or his brother's murder were willing and able to travel to Veracruz, where XXXX had been for a period of time, to locate him, let alone harm him.15 The RPD noted that while XXXX may have had fearful incidents, including the tragic death of his brother, when he was asked who these people were, XXXX did not know or speculated who they were based on rumour.16

XXXX argues that it is speculative that he would not be subjected to a risk of harm, and he submits that there is no real evidence that the risk mentioned would not be present. XXXX submits that there is not a guarantee of the absence of risk, and that the IFA would increase the risk to his entire family. XXXX argues that organized crime networks hardly leave any visible traces or evidence. XXXX argues that he is a victim of organized crime and does not carry proof of the identity of the organization. He argues that identification is the obligation of the Mexican authorities, and to pursue clarifying the identification of those responsible for his brother's death would incite and increase the actual risk.

I do not accept XXXX arguments for the following reasons. It is not the RPD's or the RAD's responsibility to refer to evidence that guarantees an absence of risk in the proposed IFA. Rather, as stated at the outset of this section, it is XXXX burden to establish that there is the requisite likelihood of harm in the proposed IFA. XXXX argues that he does not have proof of the identity of the organization, and that proving identity is the obligation of the Mexican authorities. However, this leaves XXXX with only his speculation as to the agents of harm, and also speculation whether they have the motivation and ability to pursue him in the IFA of Merida. Speculation is insufficient to meet the required standard of there being a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk of section 97(1) harm in Merida.

The RPD member decided that there was little, if any, credible evidence that XXXX profile would be of interest to the agents of harm, and that the first prong of the IFA test had not been met.17 XXXX argues that there is insufficient evidence that the agent of harm would not be interested in pursuing him to Merida or to his entire family. I do not accept XXXX argument for the following reasons. First, XXXX is attempting to reverse the burden. Once an IFA is proposed, it is XXXX burden to establish that he faces a serious possibility of persecution, or on a balance of probabilities, a section 97(1) risk in the IFA. It is not the RPD's burden to establish that he would not face such a risk. XXXX has not established that he faces a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a section 97(1) risk in the IFA of Merida. In fact, XXXX submitted an article from CNN to the RPD entitled, "Mexico Drug War Facts", updated August 27, 2019, that indicates that La Familia Michoacana (the organization that XXXX speculates is the alleged agent of harm) is "Based in the Michoacan state. Possibly defunct as of 2011. It announced it would disband in 2010, but some cells are still active in Guerrero and Mexico states, according to the Congressional Research Service report."18 The proposed IFA of Merida is not in Michoacan, Guerrero or Mexico state, but is instead located farther away in Yucatan state.

The RPD member decided that after six months of hiding, things were quiet and XXXX went back to work in the fall of 2016. The RPD noted that the noise that XXXX heard, which triggered his flight from Mexico, happened almost two years later in XXXX 2018. The RPD indicated that there were no incidents leading up to that time, and that XXXX does not know who caused the commotion he heard at his parents' place that caused him to flee.19 XXXX argues that there were no incidents because he escaped and ran for his life, and made it to a safe destiny. I do not accept XXXX argument for the following reasons. First, XXXX is speculating that the noise he heard was someone coming to harm him. He does not know the source of the noise he heard in XXXX 2018, and he is speculating when he suggests he did not receive any threats prior to then because he was in hiding. As noted by the RPD, he had left hiding to go back to work in the XXXX of 2016. He then went about his daily life without incident until he heard a loud noise in XXXX 2018.

The RPD member indicated in her decision that she reviewed the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Mexico, and noted information about Mexico and the proposed IFA of Merida.20 XXXX argues that the NDP for Mexico might not be up to date and needs to be reviewed. I do not accept XXXX' argument for the following reasons. First, he has not provided any submissions why he believes any of the specific information cited by the RPD is in error. Second, he has not provided any information of his own, either other studies or articles included in the NDP or not included in the NDP, that demonstrates how any of the specific information cited by the RPD is in error.

The RPD member referred to information in the NDP that indicates that Familia Michoacana is reducing in power and that the cartel does not have a presence in the IFA.21 XXXX argues that the Familia Michoacan leader might be replaced by another one. I do not accept XXXX argument for the following reasons. First, he is speculating that there might be a new leader. Second, he is speculating that if there is a new leader it would mean that the cartel would then develop a presence in the IFA of Merida. I must base a decision on evidence, not speculation.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
